case_mappings.clinical_pattern: A 68-year-old woman develops severe left arm pain without recalled trauma. Pain is aggravated by grasping, lying on the arm and even light touch. Initial inspection shows no bruising, erythema, skin change or deformity. Two days later, vesicular rash appears over the lateral left forearm in the C5–C6 dermatomes. The rash later clears, but severe pain persists for at least three weeks.
case_mappings.most_relevant_topic: Shingles (herpes zoster) with persistent post-rash neuropathic pain; the case explicitly names shingles. Persistent pain after rash resolution is compatible with postherpetic neuralgia, but that term is not used in the source.

clinical_correlation: The first examination has severe pain and allodynia-like pain on light touch, but no visible rash or deformity.
The vesicular rash appears later and follows the C5–C6 dermatomes, after which the doctor identifies shingles.
The PBL links shingles to a previous chickenpox infection.
At the three-week follow-up, the rash has cleared but severe pain and major functional/quality-of-life effects remain.
The source describes the treatments prescribed during the case; these are recorded as case content, not as current treatment recommendations.

osce_framework.station: Focused upper-limb neurovascular assessment after elbow/humeral injury
osce_framework.source_status: Generated study framework based on the injury and assessment topics in the supplied Week 3 material; not an official university OSCE checklist.
checklist: Introduce yourself, confirm patient identity, explain the examination and obtain consent.
Inspect the injured limb for deformity, swelling, bruising, skin integrity and abnormal posture.
Assess distal perfusion: radial pulse, capillary refill, hand colour and temperature; use Doppler if clinically indicated as stated in the lecture.
Assess motor function with nerve-specific movements: shoulder abduction (axillary), wrist/finger extension (radial), finger abduction/adduction (ulnar), thumb IP and index DIP flexion/OK sign (AIN).
Assess relevant sensation: shoulder cap (axillary), dorsum of hand/radial distribution, medial 1½ digits (ulnar), and other sensory territories as appropriate.
Document findings and compare with the opposite limb when appropriate.
Reassess and document neurovascular status after any intervention or immobilization.
limitations: The supplied slides emphasize neurovascular assessment but do not provide a complete official OSCE script.
This framework is for study and must not replace local clinical protocols or supervision.

quality_notes: Top-level keys follow the Week 1 JSON structure, especially case_mappings and image_inventory, to reduce the risk of the website importer ignoring case content.

All five uploaded PDFs were reviewed: PBL case (2 pages), complementary cases (1 page), Applied Anatomy UL-II Brachial Plexus (16 pages), Applied Anatomy UL-III Arm & Proximal Forearm (50 pages), and Anatomy of Forearm (69 pages).

The main PBL identifies Besa'ad's condition as shingles. The term postherpetic neuralgia is included only as a qualified clinical interpretation of persistent pain after rash resolution; it is not a phrase printed in the PBL.

The complementary case includes an actual elbow X-ray on page 1. The fracture label should be confirmed by reviewing the radiograph; the applied anatomy lecture provides pediatric supracondylar fracture content for correlation.
The Besa'ad PBL contains no embedded rash photograph. An external C5–C6 dermatomal shingles image is listed as a requirement, not falsely attributed to a supplied PDF.
Applied anatomy clinical scenarios are marked as lecture scenarios, not separate university PBL handouts.
Original MCQs with no printed answers remain unanswered. The two CRITOE questions on pages 43–44 have conflicting answer text in the source and are flagged rather than silently corrected.
Generated quick recall and generated MCQs are explicitly labelled as generated and are not represented as past-paper questions.
Image files themselves are not embedded. image_asset is null so the user can add extracted images later.
Page numbers refer to PDF page numbering (1-based).
Website compatibility is aligned structurally to Week 1 but cannot be guaranteed without the website's import schema/code.
The two labelled elbow neurovascular rules and diagrams on Applied Anatomy UL-III pages 40–42 were visually checked and included in the image inventory and Quick Recall.
